transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I suppose I should just start with what's been happening lately, because it's really starting to become a problem for me. You see, I’ve always prided myself on my independence. Even at my age—I’m 86, you know—I still drive myself absolutely everywhere. I used to go down to Miami all the time, just to visit family or run errands, but recently... well, what finally made me come in today is those bridges. 

The very moment my car reaches one of those long bridges toward Miami, it’s just an immediate reaction. My chest tightens up so much I feel like I can't even take a proper breath, and my hands just clamp down on the steering wheel like a vise. It's the most awful thing. I get this sudden, overwhelming certainty that I absolutely have to get off the bridge right that very second, even though I'm driving and there is simply nowhere to go but forward over the water. It just hits me all at once, the exact second the tires hit the bridge, and I sit there gripping the wheel, feeling completely trapped. I know I have a perfectly good car and I've driven for decades, but the feeling is just so strong and so instantaneous, and I just don't know how to make it stop happening...
Has this same kind of sudden, overwhelming feeling ever happened to you in other situations, like in crowds, while flying, or even when you're not driving?

No, no, it's really just the bridges. It's funny you mention those other things, because my daughter—she lives up in Orlando—she was just asking me the same thing the other day. She said, "Mom, are you feeling this way at the grocery store?" And I told her, no, absolutely not. I can go to Publix on a Sunday afternoon when it's just packed to the brim with people, and I'm right as rain. I can stand in the checkout line for twenty minutes, chatting with the cashier, not a care in the world. And flying? Oh, I've flown all over. My late husband and I used to take trips to Europe, and I never minded the planes one bit. Even now, I wouldn't bat an eye at getting on a plane. 

It’s really, truly just when I’m behind the wheel and I see that water stretching out on both sides, and there’s no shoulder, no place to pull over. If I’m just sitting at home, or walking around the neighborhood, or even driving on a regular highway where there's solid ground underneath me, I feel completely fine. I don't get that tight chest or that terrible trapped feeling at all. It's so specific to those long bridges down to Miami. I was trying to explain it to my neighbor, Martha, just last week when we were having coffee on the lanai, and she couldn't quite grasp it either. She asked if I was afraid of the water itself, but I love the ocean! I've lived in Florida for forty years. It's just... it's the bridge. Being on it, in the car. Nowhere else.

When you're on the bridge and experiencing that tightness in your chest and the urge to get off immediately, does this feeling ever escalate into a full panic attack, where you might feel like you're losing control or having heart palpitations?

Well, you know, it's... it's hard to say if it's a full panic attack, because I don't really know all the medical definitions of these things. I mean, my heart certainly beats faster, yes, absolutely. I can feel it thumping away in my chest, right under my ribs, just thump-thump-thump, like a bird trapped in a house trying to get out the window. And that tight feeling, it's so uncomfortable, like someone put a heavy dictionary right on my breastbone. But as for losing control... well, I'm driving, you see? I have to stay in control. I have my hands gripped so tightly on that wheel, my knuckles go completely white. I was looking at my hands the last time it happened—just staring at my own knuckles—and thinking, "Evelyn, you are going to break your own fingers if you don't loosen up." But I couldn't. I just couldn't let go. 

So I suppose I don't lose control of the car, thank goodness, because that would be a disaster, wouldn't it? Plunging off the side or hitting another car... oh, I can't even bear the thought. But inside my own mind? I suppose I do feel a bit like I'm losing control of my own reactions. I just sit there thinking, "Get off, get off, get off," over and over again, like a broken record. And I'm sweating, too. My palms get so clammy, which makes gripping the wheel even harder, if you can believe it. I have to keep wiping them on my slacks, one at a time, very carefully, because I don't dare take both hands off the wheel for even a fraction of a second. It's just a miserable, miserable experience, doctor. It really is. I just feel so trapped, and my body is doing all these things—the sweating, the thumping heart, the tight chest—and I can't just pull over and tell it to stop. I have to keep driving until the bridge is finally over, and it feels like it takes hours, even though I know it's only a few minutes.
Between these bridge-driving episodes, do you find yourself worrying about having another episode or actively avoiding driving over bridges?

Well, yes, I suppose I do worry about it. Actually, more than just worrying, I've... I've started changing my plans because of it. And that's really the hardest part to admit, doctor, because as I said, I've always been so independent. I have my bachelor's degree, you know, and back in my day, that really meant something. I was always the one organizing the trips, driving the carpool, handling all the logistics. But now... well, just last month, there was this wonderful gallery opening down in Miami. A local artist I've followed for years was showing her new watercolors, and I had the invitation sitting right there on my kitchen counter for weeks. I even bought a new blouse for it—a lovely shade of peach, very flattering. But when the day came, I just... I looked at my car keys, and I thought about that bridge, and I just couldn't do it. I called them and said I wasn't feeling well, which was a fib, of course, but I was just too embarrassed to tell them the real reason. 

And it's not just the gallery openings. My birdwatching group—we've been going out every second Tuesday for over a decade—they planned an excursion to a sanctuary that required crossing one of those long causeways. I had to tell them I had a conflict. A conflict! At 86, what conflict could I possibly have? And my daughter, the one in Orlando... sometimes she asks me to meet her halfway for lunch, down near the coast, and I find myself making excuses unless she offers to drive us over the water. It's humiliating, really. I’ve always been the one who planned and handled things myself, and now I'm turning down visits with my own flesh and blood just to avoid a stretch of concrete over some water. I sit at home on those days, looking out the window, feeling perfectly healthy but completely trapped by this silly fear. It just isn't like me at all.
Do you feel that your reaction to driving over bridges is more intense than the situation actually warrants, and have you felt this way for a long time?

Oh, absolutely. I know it's completely irrational, and I think that's what makes it so terribly frustrating for me. I mean, I know perfectly well those bridges have been there for years and years. My late husband used to say they were absolute marvels of modern engineering, and he was right! Thousands and thousands of people cross them every single day—commuters going to work, tourists heading down to the Keys in those giant rented RVs, delivery trucks carrying groceries—and they all get to the other side just fine. The bridges certainly aren't falling down. 

But when I'm sitting there in my Buick, and I just think about driving over all that open water, with just the sky above and the bay below... well, the fear just feels so much bigger than the actual danger. It’s completely out of proportion. I sit there and argue with myself, I really do. I say, "Evelyn, you are an educated woman, you have a college degree, you know this structure is perfectly safe." But the fear just doesn't listen to reason, does it? It doesn't care about logic or engineering. 

And as for how long it's been going on... well, it's been a while now, I suppose. It certainly didn't happen overnight. Years ago, back when the girls were young, I'd drive over those causeways without a second thought. We'd go to the beach every weekend! But then, maybe a few years back, I started noticing I'd get a little tense. I'd turn off the radio so I could concentrate, or I'd make sure I was strictly in the center lane, gripping the wheel a bit tighter than usual. And then it just kept growing and growing, like a weed in the garden that you ignore until it's completely taken over the whole flowerbed. 

Now it's at the point where my body reacts like there's a wild animal in the car with me, even though my brain knows it's just a regular stretch of paved road over the water. It's just exhausting, doctor. It really is. Knowing you're perfectly safe but feeling like you're in some kind of mortal peril all at the same time... it just drains the life right out of you.
